title: Reviewing Digital Art in 3Q 2025
body:
Peter Bauman: Hello, everyone, and welcome to this Le Random podcast at the end of the third quarter of 2025. I'm your host, Peter Bauman, the editor in chief at Le Random. Today, very luckily, we are joined by thefunnyguys, the co-founder and CEO of Le Random, and Conrad House, the collection lead at Le Random. Today, we're going to look back at the third quarter, review it, think about what some of the big picture topics and items were. We're also going to talk about some of our favorites and what we were up to this quarter. Then at the very end, we'll look ahead a bit. There was a lot that happened this quarter. We're going to talk about the rise of the digital scene at the Toledo Museum of Art, how Sasha Stiles debuted at MoMA, the restructuring at Christie's and their digital department, and then our very own thefunnyguys will talk a bit about Raster and its relation to Le Random. Then finally, we will talk about the rise of the Solana Avant art scene, especially what's happening now on VVV. A lot to talk about, a lot to discuss, and we're very excited. So let's begin.

I guess let's start with the big picture takeaways from this quarter. It felt like a lot was going on this quarter. One of the major developments, and this was due to the opening of Infinite Images at the Toledo Museum of Art in Toledo, Ohio. I knew that was coming, so that wasn't a huge surprise. But what's been more of a surprise was this continued programming around the digital. It really seems like moving forward, it's going to be something that they're going to prioritize. That was maybe a bit that I didn't expect. I think that's one of the most interesting things that happened this quarter, that Toledo is now one of the major players, it seems, in the institutionalization and presentation of digital art. But what do you guys think?

Conrad House: I think it's quite interesting to see Toledo becoming such a heavy-hitting figure. I think it's great to see they're not just stopping at Infinite Images to some degree, but they're adapting to the broader space and seeing other ways that they could fit in. I think that's really important. I think a lot of us in this space feel that the space is underrepresented to some degree. So having anybody that's here to help push us along the stage and give us a bit more spotlight is always nice to have.

And I think there is a lot of excitement about Infinite Images. I think we even talked about it at the end of our Q2 review, a lot of things that we were looking forward to. I think it lived up to a lot of the expectations that it had. It was great to see the reception of it. It was great to see Frieze and other larger publications write about the exhibition. I think it gained a lot of praise for what it showed, from the connections of our digital space to the 1960s with their Albers and Max Bill pieces that they had included. It's great to see them continue to push forward on this digital front. It's great to see that Toledo is taking that effort to become one of the leading figures in it.

thefunnyguys: Yeah, and hopefully it's also the start of seeing more physical installations for this Web3 native generation of digital artists, because I think a lot of them have ideas for physical structures and projects like that. They typically don't have the resources, or they don't get the space, or they don't know how to reach the audience in physical spaces with these projects. I think some artists in the exhibition really took good advantage of the opportunity. The one that really stood out to me was DEAFBEEF, his Glitch Box, a physical sculpture where people can physically interact with the parameters. That looks fantastic. I'm really sad I missed the exhibition. That would have been an amazing piece to interact with.

Peter Bauman: I think that's a good point about these institutions showing what their value can be, because sometimes they can be questioned in this space. Do we need them at all? I do think that they're showing that they can be valuable with what they are doing in Toledo and what they're doing also at MoMA. A lot of that is giving this digital scene a physical space, giving it a physical presence.

That was something that I spoke to Sasha Stiles and Martha Joseph, the associate curator at the Department of Media and Performance at MoMA, about in a piece at Le Random. That was just about translating this concept of a living poem into an experience in a space. Sasha even said something talking about the wall and the physical space, the work as this embodied performance that was immersive and also participatory. She said, "Part of it is thinking about the wall and this amazing screen in the MoMA lobby as a performer itself and a next-gen poet that is here to retell this AI epic."

Really incorporating the space into the telling of her story. It also allowed for them to add sound and a noise component to the space. What's also interesting is that it doesn't really take away from the more ephemeral aspects of it, because you can also engage with this work on your browser too. But it still has this space, and it still is this opportunity at the moment that will be engaging visitors, or every visitor that walks by that lobby.

Conrad House: It's the same line of thought with Toledo. It's really encouraging to see these larger institutions put forward effort and, what you said, Peter, give actual physical space to these artists. And a lot of times, physical spaces are not all equal. Obviously, when you look at things like the infamous Tezos pole compared to a MoMA screen, just because something gives it physical space doesn't mean it's done in the right way. But seeing MoMA do, obviously starting with Refik and then moving to Rafael, and then now Sasha, all three seem to be executed really well, and the works that are within the space fit really well.

It's great to see the breadth of work that they're showing. They're showing very easily appealable Refik to some degree with this very complex data cloud structured piece. And then you go to a very, I think, minimalist opposite of Refik's work with Rafael with these hard edge geometrical compositions. And then you get to also highlight another side of generative art, which is this text-based literature, which is really fascinating. And then also highlighting more AI or machine learning fields with Sasha as well.

thefunnyguys: It also feels to me like with all of these North American museums that we discussed, it's not a one-off anymore. It's not an experiment anymore. Ryan Zurer is on the boards at MoMA. The Toledo Museum of Art has started its own Labs division to encourage experimentation and invite digital artists for residencies. LACMA also announced this Digital Leaders program. These are all structural changes. These are structures that will continue to be in place at least for years, maybe for decades. It's a very different type of engagement than what it was in 2021, when NFTs and digital art were this whole thing that they just wanted to touch on for the attention and stuff. Now those structural shifts have really happened at these museums over the last years.

Peter Bauman: Yeah. I think one of the other things that presenting this work in a museum context allows is that it can have these conversations with the museum's collection. And when it's a place like MoMA, then it's conversations with art history. Sasha is doing exactly that. She told me about how the piece is in conversation with people like Bruce Nauman and Barbara Kruger and Cy Twombly, and they all have significant work at MoMA. And like you mentioned, Conrad, it was this opportunity to also show that side of text-based generative art and the language art side of it. I think that it shows the maturity of the space and has definitely been a positive development.

Well, I think if those are two positive institutional developments, maybe something... Well, I don't know. This has divided the community in terms of how they've read these tea leaves of the Christie's digital art restructuring. Some people read it that now digital art not being separate and being part of normal evening sales, that that will be overall a positive thing. There will no longer be this artificial distinction between digital art and real art or whatever that is. And now it will all just be together, although that has been done before to, I guess, varying levels of success. But how did you all interpret that news? And what did you think of that conflicting signal in this quarter?

thefunnyguys: I don't know to what extent we should feel saddened or not about Christie's not paying attention to digital art. I feel like with these type of auction houses, it's always more like a lagging indicator of relevance. It's not any predictor. They're late to the party. They come when things already have a big market, when they can make money. And once that goes away, I guess it makes sense for them to allocate less resources to the digital art sphere.

For me, it doesn't interact at all with the excitement around digital art. If anything, I feel like it's sometimes more interesting when these auction houses are not there or not in the news every week with digital art sales. I feel like, especially this quarter as well, we have seen a lot of bottoms-up movements with new collections, new artists entering the space with prices that are very affordable. That always feels like an energizing moment where real things are happening. A digital art sale at Christie's, I don't know how big of a loss it really is for the digital art space.

But that's maybe from my perspective. I think from other people's perspectives, it's really important that we get validation from institutions like Christie's, and it helps mature the space. It's a different side to the story. But personally, I don't really mind that Christie's shut down its digital art department. But I also don't want to claim it's a positive thing, to be clear.

Conrad House: I think what you nailed on the head is it depends. It's a very personal thing of whether you think it's good or bad. What Jan said, it's a lot of validation. You see some artists that joke, "I would never want my work sold at Christie's or Sotheby's." And then some other artists love that, and they love to even put it in their bio like, "Oh, artist that has been shown at Christie's auction, sold at Sotheby's auction." So it's a very personal thing. Some people feel very validated by being a part of these auction houses. Some people feel they want nothing to do with it. So it's very much a personal preference thing.

And I almost agree with Jan. I don't think it's necessarily a good thing. I don't necessarily think it's a bad thing. I think if they really do plan on just merging the digital with the real auctions, or however, what you said, Peter, what even is that? What does that even mean? I don't think it's surprising, that's for sure, that this happened. I think just last year we saw Sotheby's do this same thing when they laid off a handful of their metaverse and digital art workers in 2024. Specifically, the auction houses took one of their biggest hits in 2023.

I think a lot of the time around 2023 and even 2022 was this scramble to pick up on anything that could start generating more. And as these traditional markets collapsed, we saw these things like Sotheby's really diving into the metaverse. We saw Christie's creating these digital auction things. And it was probably due to, yeah, they're chasing the penny. They're trying to keep afloat, which you can't blame them for.

But I think even when we looked at traditional markets from 2024 to 2025, the decline hasn't been as much as it was from 2023 to 2024, where I believe from 2023 to 2024 they saw a 25% to 30% decline, whereas from 2024 to 2025 we only saw, I believe it was about a 2% to 3% decline. It seems like the falling knife has stopped its speed a bit and we're hitting a bottom.

thefunnyguys: Do you think in practice it will probably mean that only a handful of top digital artists that can sell for big ticket prices will still be featured at Christie's? We'll probably see more like Refik Anadols or Beeples go through Christie's.

On their Web3 platform, I think it was called Christie's 3.0, right? Their digital arm. I must say that they did a lot of pretty strong curations, and they did feature a lot of emerging artists. Many of the prices were actually quite accessible, sometimes starting at 0.5 ETH or 1 ETH. For Le Random, we actually collected some artworks there. We collected a Minne Atairu piece at Christie's, and she's not the artist you would expect at a top auction house already. She's very much at the start of her career, I guess. They did do a good job with curation, and they did feature a lot of underrepresented voices in their curations, which will now probably not be the case anymore.

Conrad House: Yeah, I do want to just add on that too. I was going to mention that same thing. Christie's did do a really good job, I think, even compared to the other big auction houses, at actually putting together really nice curations of new work, especially work that's coming directly from artists. I think this is partially probably due to fashion being such a big hand in it, but they put together a lot of great shows with a lot of great new work.

Peter Bauman: Yeah, I think that's where the cope went a little too far, that, "Oh, actually, this is a good thing that happened." I think it's pretty clear when you hear what Sebastian Sanchez was saying, that it went from a team dedicated and allocated and working on this and thinking about this and presenting it, and the resources of a team, to just me. When you think about it like that, it's a clear downgrade in terms of the resources that they're allocating. But that is an indication and a signal of a weaker art market, especially a secondary art market. But that doesn't say to me that there's any indication that what's happening in art is less interesting, or that it's an indication that the creativity is somehow filtering away. Again, I think it would be quite the opposite.

Let's move on to the next item, I think one of the main and big picture takeaways from this quarter, whether you're at Le Random or not, which was the introduction to the space of Raster. I wasn't surprised that it captured so much mind share on Twitter, maybe as much as it did. But I would say that I was a bit surprised at how many artists posted about it and said that they were emotional seeing all their work. That genuinely did surprise me, that it seemed to resonate with such a large number of people. Did you want to say anything about it?

thefunnyguys: Yeah, it was a big quarter for me and for the entire Le Random team with the launch of Raster. As you guys know, it's something I've been talking about for years, working on for many months, together with Michael. He was a developer, the technical co-founder of Raster. And for all that time, I always had a feeling that it will probably resonate, that it hopefully solves a real problem, not just a problem that I made up in my own mind. But when it actually launched and it received that type of reception from a lot of amazing artists, collectors, curators, it was really overwhelming. I was extremely happy to see that. It definitely made it all worth it.

I think a part of it was we want to position Raster as a new digital art marketplace. We want to make the digital art market way more efficient than it currently is. And to do so, we knew we had to aggregate artist profiles. We have to bring all their work together on one central profile. We did that mostly to improve the collector experience, so the collector doesn't have to jump from one page to another to find all the work. But it, of course, also solves a big problem for artists. They all have to work with link trees. They all have to really onboard collectors in a quite painful way when their work is dispersed across so many platforms. And some of them who have the resources, like XCOPY, they've created a really beautiful portfolio website where you can find all the work. But most artists, they don't have the time, they don't have the resources to do that, to create this portfolio website. I guess Raster does that for them at scale. It makes sense that they're really happy with Raster, but it's also something I didn't expect. Really grateful with the reception.

Conrad House: Yeah, I think this is a big congratulations to thefunnyguys for getting us out there, because like you mentioned, this has been something he's thought about for years. And I've tweeted it anecdotally, but the first time we had ever met in person, we had this discussion of, hey, it would be cool to have some really good aggregator that didn't require you to go to Foundation, SuperRare, objkt, Hic et Nunc, whatever it was at that time, fxhash, Art Blocks. You had to go through 20 different hoops just to get, hopefully, what you thought was a full encompassing view of an artist's on-chain career. Coming from a collector, it was something that I think we both had always really wanted and dreamed of.

I think at the start of 2025, we started to see a few platforms try to spearhead this initiative of, let's get all of an artist's works into one place to explore it. But it still wasn't there. They're still missing, whether it was cross-chain adaptability or even just the artist's profiles weren't fully complete and they were missing certain projects or certain works, or they weren't dividing it as nicely as Raster does, where you can divide one of ones to long-form editions, you can do series work. It's a really nice breakdown. You can see all activity on one page.

Again, with what Peter said, I was also pretty surprised to see how happy artists were, the reception of artists in general, because being a collector, I was stuck in this collector mindset of, oh, yeah, I know why collectors would love this, because of all these incredible things we just mentioned. But I never really thought about why artists might like it. And what thefunnyguys brings up with, yeah, you go to an artist's Twitter page and they have a link tree that has 20 different links attached to it with different project pages and different NFT websites that they have a work on or a project on. And it can become very convoluted for them. And again, they don't all have the time to set up a really neat artist website, or even have the time to manage an artist website where they keep up with everything that they're doing. The ability for them to just be like, oh yeah, if a collector comes to me with interest in my work, I can just share my Raster link, and my Raster link will display everything that I've done in my on-chain career, is really helpful to them. It takes away a lot of the unnecessary manual labor work that comes with being an artist and having to represent yourself to some degree, or present your work in a neat, organized fashion.

thefunnyguys: You mentioned, Conrad, that the idea has been mentioned by other platforms. I wasn't the first to mention this idea of aggregating artist works. Over the years, when I thought about the idea, I always had this feeling of, it's maybe too simple, it's too obvious. Surely someone is doing this right now, and by the time we get started working on it, someone would have beat us to the market. But then the years went by and nobody really executed it well. The devil is in the details and getting the system right. It's not very easy to solve.

And the only reason that we did end up, maybe not solving it, but making a good attempt at solving it, is because of Michael. Michael Ehlsdorfer, my co-founder, he started Masterpiece in 2022. That got acquired by Kraken, and it solved some similar issues. I actually knew that he would be the person who can actually solve it, because a lot of other people I talked to, they thought they would also be able to solve it. But with him, I actually knew, yeah, he did it before. He has a system in his mind to tackle this at scale. It has been a fun journey so far, but still a lot of issues and a lot of things to improve. So it will keep ourselves busy for a while.

Peter Bauman: Yeah, I think like Conrad said, it's one of my earliest memories also of talking to you, Jan, was you mentioning this idea. And so I'm really proud that you were able to see it through on top of doing what you've done with Le Random. So really proud of you, really proud of Michael too. And overall, very impressed and happy for you guys and what you've contributed now to the space.

thefunnyguys: I appreciate it, guys. Thank you so much for saying that. Maybe later in the call we can also talk about it a little bit more, because one particular question that I've received a lot is, how does this interfere with Le Random? Is this an entirely different business or not? I would like to answer that question. We can talk about it a little bit more later in this call.

Peter Bauman: Yeah, we'll bring up Raster a little bit later. One thing that we've talked about is the institutional changes that we've observed this quarter, the continued interest from MoMA, the rising interest from Toledo, the maybe waning interest at Christie's. One thing that we haven't talked much about is just the art that's being made right now. I think one of the most interesting things that's happening this quarter, the art being made is, I think, really exciting.

That's one of the big picture takeaways of this quarter, which is not the rise of the Solana Avant, but certainly its entrance into more of mainstream prominence, or maybe slightly more and greater acceptance, especially with ETH collectors over the last few months. It's been a really exciting energy, and I think, Jan, you even alluded to it earlier with this exciting work at approachable prices. There's this energy in the scene that I think to us who are veterans of a few years, it reminds us of some of the projects that really brought us into the space and really got us excited about everything that the space is and can be. I think that's also why it resonates maybe to us, or especially with me, is that it reminds me of my roots a little.

What do you guys think about this Solana Avant scene that's gained traction, certainly, you could say, this third quarter of 2025?

Conrad House: Yeah, I think you hit it pretty good on a lot of points, Peter. But you're right. It's nothing specifically new, because Parker Ito and Remilia and Swag World and Horses and Drifella, all these projects and Mons, they've been around for some time now. It's not like they just emerged this quarter. But you're starting to see a lot more, I think, specifically the ETH crowd and maybe even some of the Tezos objkt crew start to share it, collect it a lot more than usual. Usually it was this very niche pocketed group of enjoyers of it. It was something that I was only familiar with through adjacent talks that happened in the Terraforms Discord and people like matto and people like Garden Party on Twitter that had showcased this a lot.

When I first came across it, it was very intriguing just visually to me. Trying to understand why it's so visually intriguing was a journey in and of itself. I think you mentioned it a bit, Peter, but it reminds you of the early roots of why you got into NFTs or this digital art scene in some ways, and the relationship to how it almost feels. There's some similarities to the early Hic et Nunc stage. To some degree, it's apples and oranges, but I think in another way they're very comparable, because of just the energy that is felt within this new art movement or experimental art movement.

And not just that, but also this idea that it's stuck to Solana, which is really interesting to me, because I think for a long time Solana was seen as the meme NFT scene where obviously nothing is taken too seriously there. Anything that was serious art was seen as usually Ethereum and objkt, whereas Solana was very PFP oriented, very degenerate. So it's very cool to see an actual artistic rooted scene emerging from Solana and that they're sticking to Solana too. It's the same way that the early Hic et Nunc cool kids stuck with Tezos as this part of the personality trait. They're doing the same with Solana and creating this environment for themselves. And it's really fun.

I'd love to talk a bit more on why we think it's so captivating. I think Brian talked about it in that thread that I think we mentioned actually on our Q2 review, the schizo-collage thread of why is this so intriguing. And he talks a lot about Parker Ito's early career and how Parker has been doing this for a long time. Parker's early paintings have a lot of familiar trait-maxing compositions that you would associate to his current projects.

But to me, I think the reason I find it so intriguing is, to some nature, it's almost comforting to the chronically online kids. And I think a lot of people in our space are chronically online. So when you find work that is obviously referencing so many of these online cultures and items and niches that you're familiar with, the work resonates with you in a lot of different ways. And it's so soaked in ironic imagery and memes that there's so many layers to it. It's so meta, and it can be so much more intriguing than a regular PFP project like CryptoPunks or something, where, oh yeah, I have a CryptoPunk with a beanie or a hoodie or a basic set of earrings, rather than, oh, I have a little Swag World that has a Vetements hoodie with a Chrome Hearts hat, and I have a bacon background or something that is just so out of this world. But you can almost relate to it a bit more because you're building these connections to these cultural references that have impacted you in some ways.

It's really hard to put it into words. Sometimes you see a painting that just emotionally provokes you. I think this is how the Solana Avant scene is. It's unexplainable to the outside world. But when you've been seeped in this space for so many years, it's hard to get something that gets the motors running. For me, this is something that gets the motors running again. That's what makes it so enticing for me.

thefunnyguys: I was just going to say that I haven't been as tapped in and following as closely as you guys. I'm mostly learning about this scene from having calls with you and talking about it and the stuff you guys share. But when people talk about Drifella and Mifella, they lose me along the way.

What I find interesting from, let's say, a further distance from the scene: generativity and NFTs, it has always been a part of the story. Even CryptoPunks are generative to some extent. These traits, combinations, they're algorithmically determined. We have generative art, Art Blocks stuff, which is mostly abstract art. The Solana Avant scene, or whatever the right name is, it also plays around with generativity, but it's not the typical cartoons, like the Bored Apes, and that type of generative NFT collections. It's also not these purely abstract generative art collections. But it's something in between and something that hasn't really been explored as much yet.

And it really targets painting. It has so many art historical references about the tradition of painting. And that, to me, was something I've never seen before. And the way that also connects with internet culture, it's definitely something very unique. Territory that nobody has explored over the last years. It has been fun following from a distance.

Peter Bauman: Parker Ito, his work, I think it's really incredible. Just the fact that it has these two elements, it has the formal and figurative qualities, and then all these recognizable mimetic cultural touchstones that I think for people that have grown up with the internet over the last 20, 30 years, those things mean a lot. And it speaks that language. And it speaks it in a way that it's different. It's not better or worse, but it's different in a way that the purely abstract geometric work, maybe not purely, but the vast majority of abstract geometric work on fxhash and Art Blocks do. And maybe some people prefer, maybe people will prefer, the simplicity of pure geometric abstraction.

What I really like about the Solana scene, and Conrad, you mentioned it too, is that it isn't new. I remember about a year ago talking to 113 about Remilia and Milady, and it was the first time that I had heard about it in a serious way. I had heard about it before. I looked into it a bit more deeply at that time, about a year ago. I remember being a little afraid. I remember thinking, once you look into Remilia and Charlotte Fang, I remember thinking, oh dear. Okay. Well, that's that. Then also, maybe around that time, I looked into the Solana meme coin trenches, and I was also similarly taken aback, maybe.

Putting those two things together, I think that maybe I unfairly lumped in the Solana art scene with the ETH Milady scene, and then maybe with the worst of the Solana meme coin trenches. But there's no question the art being done there by Parker, but also people like Biscuit, Tojiba and Bosch, is some of the most interesting work being done right now. Jared Madere called Drifella 2 the most interesting painting conversation in the last 30 years. This isn't somebody who, I think, says that flippantly. This is somebody who actually knows a lot about the painting of the last 30 years, him and Parker. I really think that what's happening with Jared and Worm and Parker and Biscuit and all these guys, VVV, is exciting to me and very refreshing.

One of the reasons that I think it's also interesting is that, again, I think you can't help but compare it to some of those earlier movements that originally got us into this space. I wonder from you guys, how do you think that this Solana Avant compares and contrasts to... What is the best comparison? Is it fxhash? Is it Hic et Nunc? Is it Art Blocks? Maybe we can start there. And then how does it compare and contrast?

Conrad House: In a lot of ways, it's apples to oranges. They're almost uncomparable because it's a whole new thing in and of itself. And like you said, the roots from the Remilia scene or the Solana degen trenches scene, the way that it emerged is completely unique compared to maybe the way fxhash or Hic et Nunc emerged. But I think mine is just, yeah, what I mentioned before. I think the thing that is so... is this hardcore nature to stick to Solana and this being their home. And this is where the Avant scene is happening. And anything remotely similar to this movement is all happening on Solana. We're not seeing it happen really on ETH that much, and we're not seeing it happen on Tezos that much. I think that's what makes it so reminiscent of things like fxhash and Hic et Nunc, is that it's created its own home chain to some degree. And it's really boosted that chain's art scene just because of this one movement. So the same way that Hic et Nunc boosted the Tezos scene and fxhash boosted the Tezos scene and Art Blocks boosted the ETH scene, it's its own homegrown, I think, unicorn to some degree. So I think that's where I see the most similarities.

Peter Bauman: What I think is the main difference is the people that it's attracted. So I think that the fxhash and Art Blocks crowd attracted artists, engineers, and engineers who were creative and experimentalists and wanted to then explore with the blockchain, but probably, for the most part, didn't have a huge background in something like traditional art history or painting, or even, I would say, contemporary art for the most part.

But I would say that what this VVV scene in particular has brought is people with a painting background and people who love painting, people who understand painting and that composition. They brought that energy. That's a different artistic energy than maybe what more of an engineer brings. I don't know if it's cooler. I wouldn't say it's more authentic, but there's something about it that people who not only understand painting, but then can translate that, like Biscuit does with Drifella 2 and Drifella III, into collections that both essentially have 10,000 pieces, is, I think, a real display of talent that, again, I haven't maybe necessarily seen.

And I also think if you're not really familiar with the space, it's maybe easy to look at one Drifella and dismiss it, or just the entire collection, or just the name. Oh, it sounds... Drifella 2. But there's a one, and what is Mifella, and what is Drilady? Once you get bogged down in all that, it's easy to be like, I'm out. But if you stick with it and if you can try to meet it at its level, I think it's incredibly rich and rewarding and exciting. Like Jared said, most interesting painting conversation in the last 30 years with Drifella 2. I don't know. I don't know enough about painting to make that statement, but I think it's definitely some of the most interesting generative, coded work that's come out over the last few years.

thefunnyguys: One thing that's also really interesting, I think, to see is that I think in general, the Art Blocks, fxhash crowd, a lot of people are... Maybe it's because of the type of art, but it might also be because of the Ethereum infrastructure. But a lot of people are in their 30s, 40s. You're an outlier if you're younger than 30, I would say. If you're 27, you're one of the young guys. But I believe Jared was saying that a very large part of the user base is between the age of 16 and 23. And that to me was mind-boggling. We don't really have digital art collectors that young anywhere else. Also in long-form gen art, people are typically quite a bit older.

And I think there's many different reasons for that. I think it's the way that... there's memes in these collections, but also the accessibility of the Solana network. They have really good wallet providers like Phantom. Transactions are basically for free. A lot of these collections were distributed almost for free or for a few dollars. That's the type of stuff that someone who's 16 can actually buy into with just a bit of pocket money. They can't afford an Art Blocks mint. It's like a gas war where you need to have hundreds of dollars just to have a shot at getting a piece.

I think a lot of this chat we've talked about, just in regards to the Solana scene, the chronically online nature of the space we live in and the almost forced nature of us wanting to keep pushing every part of our life into this digital space. But it was nice to read this DEAFBEEF article. He takes a step back where he talks about the electricity and the iron, and he likes the feel of it. He likes the smell of it. He likes the way that working with these physical materials changes his psychological way and how he wakes up thinking in different ways. It was a really fascinating piece.

Again, I think also thefunnyguys mentioned it, but it was one of his favorite pieces of the Toledo show. I would also resonate the same thing, with the Glitch Box physical installation being incredible and the ways that he created his own fine-tune board where you can adjust the parameters, and seeing videos of young kids at this really barbaric iron machine, messing around with it and seeing their enjoyment was really fascinating. That article was really great. I think DEAFBEEF is just always fascinating to hear from. Anything from him is always going to be at the top of my list.

thefunnyguys: Yeah, I'm going to highlight the interview you did, Peter, with Minne Atairu. I feel like in general, her practice is super interesting. She uses AI in a quite unique way. There's not that many artists who are using AI as a tool for activism, as you described in the article. She definitely has more of a critical lens of the technology. She investigates the biases, racial, cultural biases. Besides her work with the braids, which I think you talk about quite a bit in the article, she has created quite a few very interesting AI collections. I remember her project with the Benin Bronzes, for which she won the Global South Lumen Prize a few years ago. So it was a really interesting way to use AI to basically reconstruct lost artistic heritage of a region. There was also her early work that she minted on Foundation where she had created this custom-trained AI model using makeup editorials from Instagram, which I thought was really terrific. I think the article, the interview that you did with her, was a really good insight into the way she thinks about her practice. It's quite rare. She's not that widely featured. She doesn't talk that much in depth about her practice. I'm really happy that we got to give her the opportunity to talk about her practice to our audience.

Peter Bauman: Thanks for the kind words. She's someone top of mind when I think of people that are really using some of those generative models in a compelling way that often gets flattened and overlooked.

Well, we've been talking for a lot, but I guess it was a busy quarter, and we can talk about maybe what we're looking forward to coming up in just the last minute or two. The main thing for Le Random would be, I think, in terms of physical appearance and where we'll be supporting something in person, it's FEMGEN 4 in Paris during Art Basel, and it is October 21st. We're supporting it. There's a really great list of contemporary artists involved: Gretchen Andrew, Hermine Bourdin, Saeko Ehara, Jake Elwes. And then we have Copper Giloth, who we've mentioned. She will also be there on a panel. So we're really excited about FEMGEN 4.

And then just for the rest of the year, for me, on the editorial side, I'm really excited about sinking my teeth more into that Solana Avant scene from an editorial perspective. So there's going to be... It's coming. And then I'm also looking forward to our London Art Guide that's going to coincide with Frieze London. Also keeping my eye on that NeurIPS conference in December. But it'll be a big fourth quarter, undoubtedly, too. But what are you guys looking forward to?

thefunnyguys: For me, it's also FEMGEN, Peter. I'm really excited for that. I think Art Basel Paris is going to be a great one, not only for FEMGEN and Artverse. I think the generative art crew in France is also going to do something really interesting with William Mapan, Florian Zumbrunn and a few others. So I'm quite excited for that week. It's a good reminder that I need to book my accommodation and my train tickets.

Conrad House: Yeah, I'm more on the artwork side. I'm really excited for a collection that is actually releasing today or tomorrow as of the time of recording, which is Riffs by Hash Runner, which is a new protocol-based art series where he's basically decompiling/compiling Solidity code into these bytecode compositions of different ASCII forms, which is really wonderful. I think in previous quarter talks we've talked about protocol art a bit more, in our excitement for it, to see people dive into it a bit more. So again, I still think it's a very unexplored region of this digital art space that we're in, and people are really taking the time to work with the literal contracts that they have at their hands to create new interactive protocol art. So this is really exciting. The pieces that we've already seen emerging look really great and just cool, very conceptual project by Hash Runner.

And then in terms of exhibitions, what I'm looking forward to is the Gysin-Vanetti Bear Systems exhibition that is going to be happening at the MUD Shanghai, which is curated by Mimi, actually. Again, I love that duo. I love whatever they create, so I'm sure whatever they come out with in Shanghai is going to be incredible. And look forward to seeing pictures that arise from that event.

Peter Bauman: Yeah, amazing. I think the fourth quarter of 2025 and Marfa, Miami, Basel, there's always stuff to look forward to. Big events. Well, guys, quarter three was big. It was a lot to digest, but I always enjoy doing it with you guys, with you as a sounding board, and to bounce some of these ideas off. So thank you all very much. And thank everybody for listening. And we'll see you soon.

thefunnyguys: Thank you, Peter. Thank you for hosting us. Bye, guys.

Conrad House: Bye, guys.
